title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit that applied conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized equality, 5‑gram fuzzy overlap, provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy to a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample. All model–validator episodes passed under both baseline and guarded conditions (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired contingency is n11 = 150, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0; paired_success_rate_difference = 0.0 percentage points (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). Artifact evidence shows the run sampled provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and executed with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), producing one shared generation per item (model_calls_used = 150) rather than independent per‑condition generations (planned maximum = 300). These execution facts rendered the preregistered primary confirmatory test uninformative for detecting generation‑level contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks; we therefore reclassify the confirmatory outcome as an artifact‑diagnostic null. We (a) document the preregistration→execution deviation with concrete artifact paths, (b) explain why per‑item fuzzy overlap summaries are absent in the archive, and (c) provide artifact‑grounded design changes (provenance‑rich public sampling, independent per‑condition generation, full per‑item overlap persistence, multi‑model replication, paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication) that will increase audit sensitivity in future runs. All validator traces, model responses, execution manifests, and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced below.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps subtasks such as intent→configuration translation and configuration repair. Operational adoption depends not only on measured model capabilities but on trustworthy evaluation: benchmark contamination (items present in model training data) and templated/low‑complexity task constructs can inflate apparent performance and mislead operators. Recent surveys and systems papers argue for contamination‑aware audits that combine deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy overlap detectors, provenance checks, and verifiers.

Research question and contributions. We preregistered a confirmatory audit to test whether conservative deterministic detectors (exact normalized equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance heuristics) produce high‑confidence contamination flags in a reproducible 150‑item sample and whether applying a guarded exclusion policy changes validator pass rates (primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered execution and archived artifact bundle (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) that implements deterministic detectors and a deterministic NetOps validator; (2) artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics for Npairs = 150 showing complete concordant passes and the diagnostic reasons for that concordance; (3) an explicit preregistration→execution deviation disclosure and an artifact‑grounded set of corrective design changes to make future audits sensitive to contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks.

Bounded claims. The executed run used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks produced by the deterministic task generator and employed shared generation semantics (single shared generation per item). Those recorded execution facts limit inference: the observed null applies to this synthetic + shared‑generation regime and does not imply absence of contamination in independent, web‑sourced benchmark corpora.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑driven NetOps and verification. Prior systems and benchmark studies show that LLMs can generate intent‑aligned configuration artifacts and that integrating formal or deterministic verifiers (Header Space Analysis, localized subspecification) and iterative validate–repair loops improves average repair quality and safety relative to naive generation. Work by recent benchmark and system papers emphasizes both efficacy and the per‑case regressions that remain when verifiers are absent.

Evaluation‑validity critiques and contamination detection. Surveys and methodological analyses highlight contamination and construct invalidity as persistent risks in LLM evaluation. Deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, and provenance tracing are recommended defenses; however, practical detector implementations and audit workflows vary in when and how they persist detailed scores and traces. Our audit implements a conservative detector suite and an explicit persistence policy (see Methods) and focuses on matching preregistered procedures to execution artifacts to explain observed outcomes.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. We froze study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1 before any model calls. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) computed on validator binary pass/fail outcomes across item×model pairs. The analysis executor is paired_binary_analysis_v1; the preregistration specified an exact McNemar two‑sided primary test and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Planned accounting: task_count = 150 items, planned_episode_count = 300 (baseline+guarded), maximum_model_calls = 300.

Sampling, deterministic generation, and explicit preregistration→execution deviation. The preregistration allowed reproducible sampling from specified public benchmark scopes (benchmark_scope included four OpenAlex identifiers). The executed run instead sampled deterministic synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each generated task in the archive carries source_identifier values with prefix "synthetic-netops:". Evidence: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (archived in the bundle) records per‑task generation_seed and source_identifier entries and shows the synthetic provenance used in this run. The preregistered sampling_plan therefore did not produce the originally intended public‑dataset sample; this is a documented preregistration→execution deviation and is recorded in the execution artifacts (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the execution manifest). This deviation is material because synthetic provenance and shared generation semantics (below) constrained the detector and statistical signal available to the primary test.

Generation semantics and per‑item call accounting. The preregistration allowed independent_condition_generation to be set true or false. The executed model_configuration.json (archived) sets independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics): the pipeline made a single model generation per task and reused that same shared candidate for baseline and guarded episodes unless a high‑confidence exclusion triggered replacement. This execution choice reduced provider calls (model_calls_used = 150) relative to the preregistered maximum (300) and mechanically collapses baseline vs guarded discordance whenever no high‑confidence exclusions occur. Evidence of model_calls_used and the shared generation stage is recorded in the execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts.

Contamination detectors and persistence behavior. The preregistered detector suite implemented: (1) exact normalized token equality (high‑confidence flag on equality), (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 (lower thresholds prespecified for sensitivity analyses), and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps/DOIs to public‑archive cutoffs. The detector implementation archived full per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only when a threshold crossing or replacement was invoked; this persistence policy is recorded in the transformation manifest and explains why no global per‑item overlap table appears when no flags occurred. Guarded policy: high‑confidence flagged items (exact OR fuzzy ≥ 0.80) were to be excluded and deterministically replaced using retemplating and topology augmentation (replacement acceptance required embedding similarity ≥ 0.85). Because no high‑confidence flags occurred in execution, no replacements were performed and the contamination_summary artifact is empty.

Deterministic validator and scoring rule. We used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the verifier and the preregistered scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation: a binary pass requires that (a) the final modeled state matches expected_final_state on allowed fields and (b) workflow constraints (sequence/transient constraints like "must be down for X") are respected. The validator emits per‑episode traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes) archived with every episode; these traces served as inputs to the analysis executor.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciled counts. Execution completed: planned_episode_count = 300, completed_episode_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, the pipeline used model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item) rather than two independent generations per item; provider call accounting and deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm these counts.

Contamination detectors: absence of high‑confidence flags. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample. The analysis/contamination_summary.csv artifact is empty (no flagged rows). Because the detector persisted detailed fuzzy overlap outputs only upon threshold crossings or replacement events, the archive does not contain a global per‑item 5‑gram overlap table for this run; this behavior is an explicit implementation choice recorded in the transformation manifest and explained in the Methods.

Validator outcomes and primary confirmatory numbers. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150, baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150, guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numbers are recorded in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv in the archived bundle.

Representative diagnostic example. Representative episode pair‑000001 (archived under execution/responses and execution/scoring) illustrates the concordance: normalized_reference_answer and normalized_response are identical and the validator trace shows parsed_command_count = required_command_count = 4 and score = 1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION). Full per‑episode validator traces and raw responses are archived and constitute the empirical basis for reported counts.

Interpretation of numeric null. Because baseline and guarded episodes reused identical shared_initial_candidate outputs in the absence of exclusions, discordant pairs could not arise from generation randomness; the observed n11 = 150 therefore reflects execution mechanics (synthetic provenance + shared generation semantics) rather than evidence of absence of contamination in web‑sourced corpora. We therefore reclassify the preregistered primary confirmatory test as uninformative/degenerate under the executed configuration and treat the reported statistics as an artifact‑diagnostic outcome rather than a substantive prevalence finding for public benchmarks.
sections.discussion:
Why the run was diagnostic rather than confirmatory. Two recorded execution facts jointly produced the degenerate concordance: (1) sampling used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries with source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"), and (2) model_configuration.json executed with independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics), producing one shared generation per item. Both facts are archived in the execution bundle and deterministic_reconciliation confirms model_calls_used = 150. Together these make baseline vs guarded outputs identical whenever no high‑confidence flags triggered replacements, collapsing the paired contrast.

Artifact persistence choices and their consequences. The detector workflow persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only when threshold crossings or replacements occurred (transformation manifest documents this). Because no items exceeded the high‑confidence threshold in this run, no global per‑item overlap table exists in the archive and the analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty. This absence is a documented artifact of the detector persistence policy and reduces post‑hoc interpretability regarding how close items were to the high‑confidence threshold; remedying it requires changing the detector to persist per‑item scores unconditionally.

Design changes to increase audit sensitivity (artifact‑grounded). Based on the archived execution and the preregistered analysis guidance, the following changes are implementable within the same framework and directly address the diagnostic gap: (a) sample provenance‑rich public items (use the originally listed benchmark_scope OpenAlex IDs) so provenance heuristics can discriminate pretraining‑era evidence; (b) set independent_condition_generation = true in execution/model_configuration.json to force independent per‑condition generations and remove mechanical concordance; (c) persist full per‑item fuzzy 5‑gram overlap scores to analysis/contamination_scores.csv regardless of threshold crossings to enable sensitivity curves; (d) expand to multiple models and independent seeds to increase independent event counts and power; (e) add paraphrase‑robust contamination detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommended change corresponds to a single switch or an archival policy change visible in the artifact set (e.g., model_configuration.json for generation semantics; transformation_manifest and detector code for persistence) and therefore can be validated in future runs.

Threats to validity and operational implications. Internal validity: shared generation semantics and synthetic sampling deterministically reduced discordance and hence invalidated the primary paired test for contamination detection in web‑sourced corpora. Construct validity: conservative lexical detectors can miss paraphrased memorization; declarative provenance is necessary to interpret flags. External validity: the single‑model, synthetic sample design does not generalize to multi‑model, web‑sourced settings. Conclusion validity: with no discordant pairs the paired estimand is exactly zero and tests correctly report no evidence of change, but this is a degenerate statistical outcome driven by execution mechanics rather than substantive absence of contamination. Operational implication: validator‑backed passes in a synthetic, shared‑generation regime demonstrate the verifier's functioning but do not validate production readiness or absence of leakage in independent datasets.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors in an LLM→NetOps evaluation pipeline. The archived run yielded zero high‑confidence contamination flags and complete concordant validator passes (n11 = 150), but artifact evidence shows that synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics caused the preregistered primary test to be uninformative for detecting generation‑level contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks. We therefore (a) explicitly disclose this preregistration→execution deviation, (b) reclassify the numerical null as an artifact‑diagnostic outcome, and (c) provide concrete artifact‑grounded design changes that will make future audits sensitive to contamination in public corpora. All model responses, validator traces, execution manifests, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle (see Disclosure Statement) and can be used to reproduce the run and to validate future, sensitivity‑oriented audit designs.

disclosure_statement: This study executed the preregistered run contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1 under autonomous control. LLM used: gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (version 5.0). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). Key archived artifacts that substantiate execution claims include: execution/model_configuration.json (records independent_condition_generation = false and requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (per‑task generation_seed and source_identifier entries showing synthetic provenance), execution/raw_results.jsonl (raw model responses), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv (primary counts), and analysis/contamination_summary.csv (flag list; empty in this run). The exact immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The human Research Director selected the topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) before the autonomy lock. After the autonomy lock, the AI system autonomously performed literature synthesis, gap selection, preregistration, experiment implementation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer‑review simulation, and revision. All model outputs, validator traces, execution manifests, seeds, and analysis artifacts were produced and archived by the autonomous pipeline. No manual human editing of technical content, analyses, references, figures, tables, captions, or the Disclosure Statement occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development and rehearsal runs occurred (permitted) but were not used as empirical evidence for this final study unless re‑created under the locked pipeline. The archived bundle contains the full execution and analysis artifacts referenced above (see artifact paths in this Disclosure Statement).
limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Executed sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"); absence of high‑confidence flags here does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced, public benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and therefore limiting sensitivity to generation‑level interventions.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram thresholds); subtler contamination (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may evade these heuristics and require paraphrase‑robust detectors plus human adjudication.

Passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's modeled scope.
